did_you_know.text: The heading presents the psalm as a psalm of David and dedicates it to the chief musician, the person responsible for its musical performance.
According to the heading, the psalm is connected with Nathan the prophet coming to David after the episode involving Bathsheba.
David begins by asking for mercy: he asks that his transgressions be blotted out according to God’s loving-kindness and abundant compassion.
Sin is described as a reality that David cannot escape: he says that his sin is always before him.
David acknowledges that he has sinned against God and recognizes the justice of God’s judgment, as it says: “So that You may be justified in Your words and vindicated when You judge.”
Hyssop appears here as a symbol of purification, and the request “wash me, and I shall be whiter than snow” emphasizes the desire to be cleansed completely.
The request “Create in me a pure heart” shows that the psalm is concerned not only with erasing the past, but also with bringing about inner change and renewal.
David asks for the return of the “joy of Your salvation” and for a “willing spirit” to sustain him after his sin.
The psalm emphasizes that an external sacrifice alone is not the focus of the request; David presents a broken spirit and a broken and contrite heart as the sacrifice pleasing to God.

At the end of the psalm, the prayer expands from the individual to the community: David asks for the good of Zion and the building of Jerusalem’s walls, and then describes sacrifices as an expression of righteousness.
